To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the presence of PTEN deletion was associated with shorter time-to-biochemical recurrence after radical prostate surgery, while the presence of ERG rearrangement was not.

ERG rearrangement was associated with a significantly higher rate of PTEN deletion, and that PTEN deletion, but not ERG rearrangement alone, was significantly associated with a worse oncological outcome after radical prostatectomies for clinically localized prostate cancers.

ERG rearrangement is associated with loss of the PTEN tumor suppressor gene in a significant subset of prostate cancer cases and that loss of PTEN, but not ERG rearrangement per se, is significantly associated with biochemical recurrence after prostatectomy for localized prostate cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cooperative roles of ERG and the tumor suppressor gene PTEN, in the development of prostate cancer and its progression.
the molecular basis of prostate cancer progression, with a particular interest in the role of ERG in prostate cancer progression.
the role of ERG rearrangement in the progression of clinically localized prostate carcinoma.

PTEN loss, but not ERG, is an independent prognostic factor in clinically localized prostate cancer.
ERG rearrangement does not stratify biochemical recurrence after radical retropubic prostatectomy, whereas PTEN loss is an independent predictor of biochemical recurrence.
